parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian гай (haj), from Proto-Slavic *gajь. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian гај/gaj, Slovene gaj, Slovak háj.

Borrowed from Ukrainian гноби́ти (hnobýty), from Proto-Slavic *gnobiti. According to Pokorny, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gnet-; compare Proto-Slavic *gnesti (“to press”), Proto-Germanic *knudaną.
Adaptation of Ukrainian двобій (dvobij) which, along with many other cognates, is eventually descended from Proto-Slavic *dъva (“two”) + *bojь (“fight”).

Borrowed from Ukrainian дітвора (ditvora) during XIX century, which was derived from Old East Slavic дѣтъва (dětŭva) (compare derivation of мошкара (moškara)), from Proto-Slavic *dětъva. Compare Polish dziatwa.

Borrowed from Ukrainian нудни́й (nudnýj), from Old Ruthenian нꙋдны́й (nudnýj, “boring”), from Old East Slavic нꙋдьнъ (nudĭnŭ, “gruelling, difficult”), from Proto-Slavic *nudьnъ. By surface analysis, ну́да (núda) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: glaze, glaze ice, glazed frost, verglas, sleet
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian о́желедь (óželedʹ), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)želdь, from Proto-Slavic *o(b)- + *želdь.
Borrowed from Ukrainian ха́та (xáta, “house; home”), from Proto-Slavic *xata, from Scythian.
From Ukrainian цу́цик (cúcyk), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *cucьkъ (“dog, puppy”).

Borrowed from Ukrainian череви́к (čerevýk), from Old East Slavic черевикъ (čerevikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *červikъ (“shoe”), from *červo (whence Russian чре́во (črévo, “belly, womb, inside, interior”)). Doublet of череви́цы (čerevícy), inherited directly from East Slavic.
